rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 4-5 - the authors collected their own UAV RGB imagery from three olive fields in northern Greece (Oct-Nov 2022), annotated 3038 tree instances, and trained/tested YOLOv5n/s/m models, reporting precision, recall and mAP on a held-out test set (Figure 6, Tables 3-6).
rows.notes: The study reports only detection/classification of olive trees as healthy or damaged by Verticillium wilt from UAV imagery, in the symptomatic season (late autumn when symptoms are pronounced). It does not test or report any control, prevention, or reduction of disease expansion; it only states in the Introduction that early detection 'could support' solving the problem, and early detection via thermal/NIR imagery is listed as future work. Detection is a precondition of control, so upstream=true. Note also the study concerns Verticillium dahliae, not Xylella fastidiosa as the review context implies; the technology (UAV remote sensing) matches, so technology_mismatch is left false but the disease differs. The damaged class consistently scored lower; the authors attribute this to class imbalance and few training images, which would count as limitations on detection but not on the claimed control effect.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a detection-only methods paper (YOLOv5 architecture comparison) with no results on disease control or spread reduction.
